newsitem.title: USA: Allegheny, DQE deal cheered by analysts.
newsitem.headline: Allegheny, DQE deal cheered by analysts.

text.p: The proposed merger of Allegheny Power System Inc and DQE Inc is an excellent match that will bring the combined company a more favorable customer mix, save costs and likely keep a lid on future rate increases, analysts said on Monday.
"I think it's an excellent fit because there is geographic proximity and complementary features, including customer mix," said Barry Abramson at Prudential Securities.
"Allegheny is primarily rural, DQE is urban. DQE's customer mix has a small industrial component to it and Allegheny's has a large one," he said.
"I also think there will be rate decreases as the companies work out a plan to pass through their savings," he said.

Allegheny Power, based in Hagerstown, Maryland, and Pittsburgh-based DQE said early Monday they had an agreement to merge in a tax-free stock transaction that will create a company with a market capitalization of about $10.6 billion.

DQE shareholders will receive 1.12 shares of Allegheny Power common stock for each share of DQE common stock. Allegheny Power will issue about 86.5 million shares, valued at about $2.6 billion, to DQE shareholders.

Analysts said the 23 percent premium Allegheny Power agreed to pay was in line with other utility mergers. The industry has been consolidating because of deregulation legislation that will allow customers to choose their power supplier.

"I think the premium's in line with other mergers," said Ronald Tanner at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "There are significant savings to be achieved and customers will get about half. If shareholders get the other half, that will overcome the premium. I think it's a very favorable deal."
Executives of both companies said at a news conference earlier Monday that the deal would result in about $1.0 billion in cost savings over the next 10 years.
They also said about 500 jobs will be lost as a result of the merger, with the cuts achieved primarily through attrition and early retirements. The combined workforce is expected to be about 8,500.
The companies expect the deal to be accretive to earnings and all regulatory approvals to be achieved within 12 to 18 months.
Morever, company officials said rates from the new company would be lower than if the two companies remained independent.

Analysts said they expected the deal to be approved easily because there were no antitrust concerns. "I think it's highly likely that regulatory approval will be received within a year," said Richard Sporrer at Parker/Hunter.
Allegheny Power provides electric service to nearly 1.4 million customers in parts of Maryland, Ohio, Pennsylvania, Virginia and West Virginia.
DQE's subsidiary, Duquesne Light Co, serves more than 580,000 customers in a service territory of about 800 square miles, including the city of Pittsburgh.
"The two companies abut each other; they've done deals together before," said Edward Tirello Jr. at NatWest Securities. "It makes a tremendous amount of sense from an operational standpoint."
Analysts also said the deal could result in minor rate decreases and the likelihood of increases from the combined company would be less than if the two utilities did not merge.
"I think you'll see some rate decreases, although they would be minor," Sporrer said. "I think you'll see fewer rate increases going forward."
